interactions.label: A patient develops scabies for the first time. What explains the 4–6-week delay

params.question: A patient develops scabies for the first time. What explains the 4–6-week delay before itching begins?

answers.text: The mite needs that long to establish enough burrows to cause symptoms

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The mite begins burrowing within hours of skin contact. The delay is immunological — the body needs time to develop a type IV (delayed) hypersensitivity response to mite proteins and faecal matter.

answers.text: The immune system requires time to mount a type IV hypersensitivity response to mite antigens

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. In a first infestation, the adaptive immune system takes 4–6 weeks to become sensitised. On re-infestation, the primed immune system recognises the mite immediately and itching begins within 1–2 days.

answers.text: Eggs need 4–6 weeks to hatch and produce enough larvae to trigger irritation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Eggs hatch in just 3–4 days and the full life cycle from egg to adult completes in 10–14 days. The delay is due to immune sensitisation, not the reproductive timeline of the mite.

answers.text: Mite faeces accumulate gradually over weeks before reaching an irritant threshold

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The itch is driven by an adaptive immune response (type IV hypersensitivity), not by a cumulative irritant effect. This is why first-time and repeat infestations produce such markedly different symptom timelines.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember that the itch in scabies is a type IV (delayed) hypersensitivity response. First exposure requires 4–6 weeks for sensitisation; subsequent exposures trigger itch in 1–2 days because the immune system is already primed.
The itch in scabies is immune-mediated, not mechanical. This distinction explains why first infestations are silent for weeks while re-infestations itch within days.

interactions.label: A homeless man presents with intensely itchy excoriations on his trunk. No lice

params.question: A homeless man presents with intensely itchy excoriations on his trunk. No lice are seen on skin examination. Where should you look next to confirm the diagnosis?

answers.text: The scalp hair behind the ears and at the nape of the neck

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Behind the ears and the nape are sites for head lice (pediculosis capitis). Trunk excoriations in a person living in overcrowded conditions suggest pediculosis corporis, where the body louse lives in clothing seams.

answers.text: The anogenital hair and inner thighs

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Anogenital involvement points to the pubic louse (Pthirus pubis), which spreads through sexual contact. Trunk excoriations with overcrowded living conditions are characteristic of pediculosis corporis — examine the clothing seams.

answers.text: The seams of the patient's clothing

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The body louse (Pediculus humanus corporis) lives and lays its eggs in clothing seams, coming onto the skin only to feed. Missing the clothing examination is the commonest reason for missed diagnoses of pediculosis corporis.

answers.text: The eyebrows and eyelashes under magnification

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Eyelash infestation occurs with the pubic louse (Pthirus pubis), not the body louse. In this clinical scenario — trunk excoriations, no lice on skin, overcrowded living — the diagnosis is pediculosis corporis. Always check the clothing seams.

overallFeedback.feedback: In pediculosis corporis, the body louse lives and lays eggs in clothing seams — not on the skin. If you only examine the patient's body, you will miss the diagnosis. Always check the clothing in trunk excoriations with features suggesting louse infestation.
The body louse is unique among human lice in living on clothing rather than the body. This is why treatment centres on hot-washing or ironing of clothing seams, not just topical pediculicides.

interactions.label: A young woman presents with intensely itchy, grouped vesicles over the extensor

params.question: A young woman presents with intensely itchy, grouped vesicles over the extensor surfaces of both elbows and knees. There are no burrows and no household contacts are affected. Which diagnosis should you consider instead of scabies?

answers.text: Atopic dermatitis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Atopic dermatitis favours flexural sites — the antecubital and popliteal fossae — not extensor surfaces. Grouped vesicles symmetrically over extensors point to dermatitis herpetiformis, which is associated with coeliac disease.

answers.text: Dermatitis herpetiformis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Dermatitis herpetiformis produces intensely itchy, grouped vesicles over extensor surfaces and is associated with coeliac disease. Immunofluorescence shows granular IgA deposits at the dermoepidermal junction — findings scabies never produces.

answers.text: Papular urticaria

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Papular urticaria produces grouped itchy papules on exposed skin from insect bites. The extensor distribution and vesicular morphology in this case are characteristic of dermatitis herpetiformis, not insect-bite reactions.

answers.text: Neurotic excoriation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Neurotic excoriations are self-inflicted and lack a primary lesion morphology such as grouped vesicles. The symmetrical extensor distribution with vesicles points to dermatitis herpetiformis, which warrants screening for coeliac disease.

overallFeedback.feedback: Dermatitis herpetiformis presents with grouped, intensely itchy vesicles over extensor surfaces — unlike scabies, which favours web spaces, wrists, and genitalia. It has no burrows or contact clustering, and immunofluorescence demonstrates granular IgA deposits.

Each scabies mimic is distinguished by what it lacks — burrows, web-space involvement, or household clustering — and by its own characteristic features. Dermatitis herpetiformis stands out with extensor vesicles and its coeliac disease association.

interactions.label: A patient completes two applications of permethrin 5% cream one week apart for s

params.question: A patient completes two applications of permethrin 5% cream one week apart for scabies. Ten days after the second application, itching persists but no new burrows are found on examination. What is the most appropriate next step?

answers.text: Re-treat with a third application of permethrin 5% cream

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Unnecessary re-treatment is a common mistake. Post-scabetic itch persists for 2–4 weeks after successful eradication because dead mite material continues to provoke an immune response. Without new burrows, this is not treatment failure.

answers.text: Switch to oral ivermectin as permethrin has clearly failed

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The absence of new burrows suggests the mites have been eradicated. Persistent itch without new lesions is a type IV hypersensitivity response to residual mite antigens — not a sign of treatment failure requiring escalation.

answers.text: Reassure the patient that post-scabetic itch can persist for 2–4 weeks and treat symptomatically

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Post-scabetic itch is driven by the lingering immune response to dead mite proteins and faeces. It resolves within 2–4 weeks. Symptomatic relief with emollients and antihistamines is sufficient when no new burrows appear.

answers.text: Perform a skin biopsy to determine why the treatment failed

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A skin biopsy is not indicated when the clinical picture fits post-scabetic itch — persistent pruritus without new burrows after adequate treatment. Reassurance and symptomatic care are the appropriate response.

overallFeedback.feedback: Post-scabetic itch persists for 2–4 weeks after successful treatment because the immune response to dead mite antigens takes time to subside. Without new burrows, this is normal resolution — not treatment failure. Reassure and manage symptoms.

Distinguishing post-scabetic itch from treatment failure is essential. The key is the absence of new burrows — if none are found, the mites are likely eradicated and the itch is a residual immune response that resolves in 2–4 weeks.

interactions.label: A child with pediculosis pubis is found to have lice on the eyelashes. What is t

params.question: A child with pediculosis pubis is found to have lice on the eyelashes. What is the recommended treatment for the eyelash involvement?

answers.text: Permethrin 1% lotion applied carefully to the lashes

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Chemical pediculicides like permethrin cause significant irritation when applied near the eyes. White soft paraffin (petroleum jelly) physically smothers the lice without chemical injury to the eye.

answers.text: Malathion 0.5% solution on a cotton-tipped applicator

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Malathion is an organophosphate that would cause significant eye irritation and potential toxicity. White soft paraffin applied to the eyelashes smothers the lice safely without chemical risk.

answers.text: White soft paraffin applied to smother the lice

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. White soft paraffin physically occludes and smothers the lice and is safe near the eyes. Also remember that pubic lice on a child's eyelashes should prompt consideration of possible sexual abuse.

answers.text: Oral ivermectin as topical agents cannot be used near the eyes

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While systemic treatment is an option for extensive infestation, the standard approach for eyelash lice is topical white soft paraffin — a non-irritant physical treatment that smothers the lice safely near the eye.

overallFeedback.feedback: Chemical pediculicides are too irritant for periocular use. White soft paraffin (petroleum jelly) is the recommended treatment for eyelash lice — it smothers the lice physically without chemical injury to the eye.

Eyelash lice require a mechanical rather than chemical approach — white soft paraffin smothers the lice without risking ocular irritation. Always consider the safeguarding implications of pubic lice in a child.
